cells.tense: Right now, with the pen in your hand.
cells.verb: tending what grows, with care that keeps it alive without taking it over
cells.place: in the things people share and hand down — the practices, the sayings, the ways of doing it
cells.ask: Let what you've been tending be seen on purpose — show one person what you've kept alive and why — and let one thing you've finished with go, as done rather than lost.
cells.core:
You're keeping the shared things alive, and you're doing it well. The old way and the new need are both in your hands and you're not dropping either — you keep what's proven itself and you let it grow where it wants to. What people around you inherit from this is in good shape because somebody has actually been looking after it, and the looking after doesn't wear you out.

That's not the end of anything. It's a place to feed from. The tending has mostly happened out of sight, and what you've kept going could stand to be seen as yours — not for applause, just so the care is visible. And some of what you hold has already finished its job; setting that down isn't giving up on it, it's the last part of taking care of it.
cells.sheetLine: You're keeping what's shared alive, and it's growing in your hands.

cells.tense: You're living in a future where the shared things slip unless you hold them tighter.
cells.verb: tending what grows until the tending turns into gripping
cells.place: in the practices and ways of doing things that people hand down together
cells.ask: Before you decide what else to guard, sit with how much of what you once imagined for these shared things has already come true — take that in all the way — and let that fullness be what sets your grip, so the care stops exhausting you and the holding stops clutching.
cells.core:
You're protecting what gets passed on harder than it needs protecting. Somewhere ahead is a version where it's all slipped — the ways forgotten, the meaning gone thin — and you're already bracing for it, so every change starts to look like a loss and every loose end like a threat. The care is real. It's just running on fear now, and what you're tending can feel that.

Things people share don't survive by being gripped; they survive by being lived. What you're reaching for isn't more control. It's the part you skipped — actually taking in what's already grown, how much of what you hoped for is standing in front of you. Hands that know that are steadier, and they can hold without squeezing.
cells.sheetLine: You're guarding what's shared so hard it can't breathe.

cells.tense: You're still standing at a door that's already behind you.
cells.verb: tending what grows — except the tending stopped
cells.place: in the shared practices and meanings that only keep going if someone keeps them
cells.ask: Don't force yourself back to the tending — go back to the hoping instead: name one shared thing you still believe is worth carrying forward, after everything, and keep believing it out loud; the care tends to follow the hope back in, and it comes back as growth you don't have to force.
cells.core:
You let the shared things lapse. The practices that used to carry meaning between people, the ways of doing it that held you together — they needed a hand on them and the hand came off, and something back there made coming off feel like the sane choice. Now there's a gap where the tending was, and you can see it from where you're standing.

The pull is to throw effort at the gap — resurrect everything, make up for the quiet. That kind of push tends to run dry fast. What's actually missing isn't the labor; it's the belief underneath it, the sense that this is still worth carrying. That's where the current comes back in. Hope first, and the tending doesn't have to be dragged back — it walks in on its own, and it doesn't wear you down this time.
cells.sheetLine: You stopped keeping what was shared, and you can see the gap.

cells.tense: Pen down, in a room you're already writing.
cells.verb: tending what grows, quietly, and calling it nothing
cells.place: in what gets handed down and held in common
cells.ask: Say it plainly to one person — "I do this on purpose, and I keep it going" — and let them see the intent behind the care; once it's yours in the open, you can tell which parts are done and set those down without it feeling like defeat.
cells.core:
You're already the one keeping the shared things alive. The way it gets done around here, the things that get remembered, the practices that haven't died out — those are still standing because you've been tending them, steadily, with both demands held in balance. You just don't say so. Ask you and it's habit, or it's just how things are, or it's someone else's doing.

The care is real and it's working. What's missing is the claim on it, and without the claim the holding gets heavy in a way you can't account for — you can't set anything down because officially you aren't carrying it. Letting the intention be seen isn't vanity. It's what lets the holding turn back into care instead of clutching.
cells.sheetLine: You're already keeping what's shared alive. You just haven't called it yours.
